The Master accepted it without responding. When Mencius served as a minister in Qi, he resided in Pinglu, a subordinate city of Qi. Chuzi served as the prime minister of Qi and attempted to associate with Mencius through gifts of silk; Mencius also accepted these without responding. Another day, when traveling from Zou to Ren, Mencius met Chuzi’s younger brother. However, when traveling from Pinglu to the capital of Qi, he did not meet Chuzi. Wuluzi, pleased, said: "Is it because he is now a minister?" Wuluzi saw Mencius there; because the two had different experiences regarding being met, he asked, delighted to finally have a moment to speak with the Master: "When you traveled to the state of Ren, you met the younger brother; when you went to the state of Qi, you did not meet Chuzi. Is it because Chuzi is the prime minister of Qi that you wished to slight him?"

Mencius replied: "It is not so. It is because his presentation was incomplete." Mencius answered: "It is not because he is a minister that I did not meet him to slight him. As the *Shangshu* chapter 'Luo Gao' says: 'The presentation requires many rites.' This means the rites for a formal audience require many protocols. If the rites do not match the value of the gifts presented, it is called failing to present. Because he lacked the proper rites, even though he had gifts to present, it was as if nothing had been presented at all. One in a high position should not cause his subordinates to compromise their principles for the sake of presentation. Therefore, I did not meet Chuzi because his rites were not equal to his gifts, making it an incomplete presentation. That is why I accepted his silks but did not reciprocate." Wuluzi was satisfied. Having reached Pinglu, Wuluzi already understood, and thus was pleased upon hearing Mencius’s words. Someone saw Wuluzi and asked him: "What does this passage from the 'Luo Gao' mean?" Wuluzi replied: "The younger brother was guarding the state, and therefore could not cross the border to personally go to the state of Zou to meet Mencius."

chinese-cohort-5547-1b2b4c-p81|K.text:
My five talents have been exhausted, and the two physicians <note>referring to the internal ailment and the press of circumstances</note> press upon me; mid-course, I beg to be allowed to retire, a request made without pretense or artifice.

I humbly request an imperial decree be issued to the Ministry of Personnel to approve my retirement, so that I may henceforth join the well-fed and contented populace, living under the benevolent reign of the Emperor <note>original: "Yao-tian", a metaphorical reference to the Golden Age of Emperor Yao</note> for all eternity.

Ni Yuanlu’s memorial recommending Huang Daozhou states: “In terms of both scholarship and conduct, he is the foremost among the literati and should be retained in the Bureau of Historiography. I, your humble servant, measure my own abilities and find them inferior; I earnestly beg for a change in position so that his talent may be fully utilized.” Your servant has heard that ordinary talent is easily found, while exceptional scholars are difficult to acquire. Thus, in the past, there was the remark made in the <term>Xuanshi</term> <gloss>the throne room</gloss> about having not seen such a person for a long time, and the lament regarding how one could obtain the talent of the <term>Shanglin</term> <gloss>Imperial Park</gloss> and the <term>Xing'an</term> <gloss>a pavilion</gloss> simultaneously. Even average rulers felt such earnest concern for talent; how much more so for Your Majesty, whose Neo-Confucian governance and brilliance emerge as first among the ages, where the auspicious clouds and dragon gather to meet this moment.

Volume Four

Yi (乂): To govern or manage. 

Mo (沒): To sink. In Cao Zhi’s *Seven Exhortations* (Qiqi): “Soaring like a wild swan, sinking like a mallard, following the body with swiftness, chasing the form without catching it.” (Note: The pronunciation is *di*, *di*, *qie*).

Mi (密): Quiet. Jiang Yan’s *Eulogy for Emperor Gao of Qi*: “At the royal tombs of the Song, the purple palace is hushed and still (mi).” (Note: The passage from the *Yingcui* anthology states: “The decree of the spoken word remains in the refined essence.”)

Zai (載): To board or ride. In the *Rites of Zhou* (Zhouguan), the commentary on the *Zai Shi* (Master of Chariots) says: “The word *zai* refers to affairs.” The Langya Stone Inscription of the Qin dynasty says: “Wherever the moon shines, the boats and carriages that carry (zai) them all fulfill their destiny; there is no one who does not attain their desires.” (Note: The pronunciation is *zi*, *ji*, *qie*).

Zai (再): Double or repetition. Qu Yuan’s *Nine Chapters* (Jiuzhang): “Turning my back on the laws and standards, my heart is burdened; that and this are no different. I would rather die and be cast away than fear that disaster and calamity will strike a second time (zai).”

Jie (節): Integrity or moral conduct. Cao Zhi’s *Eulogy for the Hegemons and Kings*: “Strong spirit, missing the mark; the body exerts its integrity (jie). What is conquered must be taken; plans leave behind manifest benefits.”

Ji (跡): Footprints or trace. In the *Daozang* (Taoist Canon): “Flying wheels drift through the vast sky; without form and also without trace (ji). The path of the flying wheels rises suddenly beyond the borders.”

Zhai (瘵): Sickness or distress. Mu Hua’s *Rhapsody on the Sea* (Haifu): “The heavenly net surges and boils, becoming carvings, becoming distress (zhai). The great waves overflow, vast and boundless for ten thousand miles.” (Note: The pronunciation is *zi*, *li*, *qie*).

Cai (蔡): A type of grass. 

Cha (察): To examine or discern. The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states: “The word *ji* (sacrifice) is to say *cha* (examine). To examine means to arrive. Human affairs must arrive, and only then is there sacrifice.” Wang Yi’s *Nine Regrets* (Jiuhuai): “The water sparkles; I display my flags in succession, and the clouds of Cai (a colorful banner) flutter.” 

Ban Gu’s *Rhapsody on Silent Communion* (Youtong fu): “I grasp the vines and grant them to the king; I look at the high valleys and say, ‘Do not fall.’ At dawn, I wake and ponder; my heart is cloudy and still not clear (cha).”

Zu (卒): To end or finish. Zuo Si’s *Rhapsody on the Capital of Wu*: “The tattooed warriors, the soldiers (zu) with carved bodies, adorned with dragons, horned serpents, and scaly beasts, facing each other.” (Note: The pronunciation is *jiang*, *sui*, *qie*).

Cai (菜): Edible greens. Dongfang Shuo’s *Seven Admonitions* (Qijian): “Xi Shi is beautiful, yet I cannot see her; the moth-browed ones are hurried and distracted.” (Note: The pronunciation is *qi*, *ji*, *qie*).

The clouds condense, as recorded in the *Book of Song*, Treatise on Rites. <note>A reference to the collection of rites and ceremonial observations during the Liu Song dynasty.</note> The raw, sullen smoke rises to form palaces, as described in Zhao Ang’s "Rhapsody on Duckweed." It divides into fragments, as when King Wang saw the moon rising above, everywhere suspecting them to be stars.

The clouds brush past, as in Li Yuan’s poetry. Decorating the moon, they lean against the desolate trees of the ancient city.

The clouds turn over, as in Wang Bo’s "Rhapsody on Lotus Picking." The mists converge, shining in a blurred, indistinct manner.

The clouds struggle, as in the linked verses of Han Yu’s "South of the City." How could one reach the limits of the wind and seasons? Who could ever return?

The clouds soar, as in the poetry of Bai Juyi. Crab-fires in the autumn wind; spring rains gather like stars, playing with the banners on the waves.

The clouds interlace, as in Yu Shao’s "Preface to Visiting Secretary Li’s Flower and Medicinal Garden." The towers adorn the plain walls, shining with the frost of cranes; red cassia trees flap and expand, while the smoke spreads below. Tao lifts the flower calyx, and Li displays his essence.

The clouds behold, as in Sikong Tu’s "Willows" verses. Again, the wonders of the encircling mountains; near the time of the Qingming festival, the smoke envelops the city of the prefecture.

Sequentially determined for the *Siku Quanshu* <gloss>Complete Library of the Four Treasuries</gloss>, Imperial Parallel Characters, volume fifty-five.

Once he became wealthy and strong, he then moved to Bin. The expansion began from the time Buzhu moved to the walled city, not from the move from Tai. Some say "Gong" was a title and "Liu" was a name; others say "Gong" was a noble rank or "Liu" was a courtesy name. All of these lack historical evidence.

Facing south toward the state of Chu, there were once again affairs involving the various Di tribes. This occurred because the six ministers grew stronger by the day, all harboring the ambition to richly entrench and expand their own influence. Therefore, they abandoned far-sighted strategies and pursued immediate gains instead.

Autumn. Ju Quji entered Ju from Qi. Zhaoyu of Ju fled to Wu.

Commentary: According to the <note>Zuo Zhuan</note> <gloss>The Commentary of Zuo</gloss>, the Viscount of Ju fathered Quji and Zhaoyu. Quji was the eldest, yet he was not established. Zhaoyu was established, but then deposed. If the Viscount of Ju had been murdered and Zhaoyu was then established, he would have been established by the criminals. However, he had not participated in the murder. If he could have used his position to punish the murderers, then being established by criminals would have caused no harm. Since he could not punish the murderers, he was simply a criminal himself. That Quji fled and then entered from Qi was merely an act of utilizing the power of a great state to contend for the throne; it was also not done with the intent to punish the murderers. Therefore, the records state he "entered" to highlight this offense.

Commentary: According to the <term>Zuo Zhuan</term> <gloss>Commentary of Zuo on the Spring and Autumn Annals</gloss>, the Viscount of Ju had two sons, Quji and Zhanyu. Quji was the elder but had not been established as heir. Zhanyu had been established, but then was deposed. If one were able to use the position of being installed to punish the murderers, even being installed by them would cause no injury. If one cannot punish the murderers, then one is merely a guilty party. The fact that Quji fled and then entered from Qi signifies that he was leveraging the power of a great state to contend for the kingdom. It was not done with the intention of punishing the murderers. Therefore, the text records his "entry" to show his culpability.

The tides all depend upon the moon. When the moon approaches the <term>Mao</term> <gloss>East</gloss> and <term>You</term> <gloss>West</gloss> positions, the tide rises in the east and west. When the moon approaches the <term>Zi</term> <gloss>North</gloss> and <term>Wu</term> <gloss>South</gloss> positions, the tide rises in the north and south. In a single month, the tides are greatest after the new and full moons; in a single year, the tides are greatest during the spring and autumn equinoxes. This ebb and flow of the tide depends upon the advance and retreat of the moon, and is not due to the rising and sinking of the earth. I, the humble author, believe that all the theories mentioned above differ from one another. However, the principle that "Heaven produces water first" <note>a reference to the opening lines of the "Great Commentary" on the I Ching, identifying Water with the number one</note> implies that its essence is <term>yin</term> <gloss>feminine/receptive principle</gloss> yet it is born from <term>yang</term> <gloss>masculine/active principle</gloss>. Its movement and circulation around the outside and interior of the earth perhaps cannot be attributed solely to the moon as the cause of the ebb and flow. If one believes that when the primordial <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital energy/breath</gloss> rises, the earth sinks and the water overflows, and when the <term>qi</term> descends, the earth floats and the water contracts, then since the high and low terrain of the land has remained the same from ancient times to the present, one has never actually seen it sink or float. The theory of latitude and longitude put forth by Master <term>Zhu</term> <gloss>Zhu Xi</gloss> is a grand framework for understanding the space between Heaven and Earth and the Five Elements.

The ebb and flow of tides is entirely dependent on the moon. When the moon is in the position of <term>Mao</term> <gloss>east</gloss> or <term>You</term> <gloss>west</gloss>, the tide rises in the east and west. When the moon is in the position of <term>Zi</term> <gloss>north</gloss> or <term>Wu</term> <gloss>south</gloss>, the tide rises in the north and south. Within a month, the tide is strongest after the new moon and full moon. Within a year, the tide is strongest during the spring and autumn equinoxes. This ebb and flow of the tide is therefore linked to the advance and retreat of the moon, and it is not due to the sinking and floating of the earth.

I, the foolish one, believe that the above theories are all different. However, the saying "Heaven produces water first; its substance is <term>yin</term> <gloss>passive/feminine energy</gloss> yet it is born from <term>yang</term> <gloss>active/masculine energy</gloss>" suggests that it circulates and moves outside the earth and within heaven. I fear it cannot be attributed solely to the moon as the cause of the ebb and flow. If one thinks that when the primordial <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital energy</gloss> rises, the earth sinks and the water overflows, and when the <term>qi</term> descends, the earth floats and the water shrinks, then the terrain of plains and wetlands would remain the same throughout history, and we have never actually witnessed this sinking or floating. The theory of latitude and longitude put forward by Master Zhu <note>referring to Zhu Xi</note> is a major principle governing heaven and earth, as well as the Five Phases.

Liu Houji was a great-grandson of the Lord of Millet <note>original: Houji</note>. When the rule of the Xia dynasty declined, the descendants of the Lord of Millet ceased to attend to agriculture. Bu Zhuo lost his official position and fled to the lands between the Rong and Di tribes. Bu Zhuo’s grandson, Gong Liu, although living among the Rong and Di, resumed the work of the Lord of Millet. Once he had become wealthy and strong, he migrated to Bin. This was a migration from the city of Bu Zhuo, not a migration from Tai. Regarding Gong Liu, some say "Gong" was his title and "Liu" was his name, others say "Gong" was his rank or "Liu" was his style name; all these lack historical evidence.

*“Duo”* <note>original: 篤</note>
Read following the style of this section. 

*“Gong Liu Fei Ju, Fei Kang. Nai Chang”* <note>original: 公劉匪居匪康廼場</note>
The pronunciation of *Chang* <note>original: 場</note> comes from *Ri* <note>original: 日</note> and *Xi* <note>original: 夕</note>, which is the character *Yi* <note>original: 易</note>. In the middle of the character *Yi* there is a long stroke, which makes it the character *Yang* <note>original: 陽</note>. Adding the earth radical to the side makes the sound *Chang* <note>original: 埸</note>.

*“Nai Jiang, Nai Ji, Nai Cang. Nai Guo”* <note>original: 廼疆廼積廼倉廼裹</note>
The pronunciation is *Guo* <note>original: 果</note>. 

*“Hou”* <note>original: 餱</note>
The pronunciation is *Hou* <note>original: 侯</note>. 

*“Liang Yu Tuo”* <note>original: 糧于橐</note>
The pronunciation is *Tuo* <note>original: 託</note>. 

*“Yu Nang. Si Ji”* <note>original: 于囊思輯</note>
The pronunciation is *Ji* <note>original: 集</note>. 

*“Yong Guang Gong Shi. Si Zhang Gan Ge Qi Yang. Yuan Fang Qi Xing”* <note>original: 用光弓矢斯張干戈戚揚爰方啓行</note>
Rhymes with *Hang* <note>original: 杭</note>. 

This is a poem about planning the migration. "Duo" means simple and earnest. I will detail this in each chapter. When doing a task, one must be thorough. The beginning and end of a matter must be simple and solid, without a trace of vanity, not allowing a single point of leakage. People who establish a foundation are generally like this. The word "Duo" should be read slowly. "Ju" means to reside; "Kang" means peace. Gong Liu lost his position and fled to the Rong and Di tribes, contemplating the insecurity of the people's lives and lamenting the state of the nation.

According to the <term>Zuo Zhuan</term> <gloss>Commentary of Zuo</gloss>, the Viscount of Ju fathered both Qujiji and Zhan Yu. Qujiji was the elder, yet he had not been established as heir. Zhan Yu had been established, but was subsequently deposed. By the time the Viscount of Ju was murdered, Qujiji had fled, and Zhan Yu was established; thus, he was installed by the murderers. However, he had not been involved in the regicide. If he had been able to take advantage of his position to punish the murderers, his being installed by them would have done no harm. Since he could not punish the murderers, he was simply a criminal. That Qujiji fled and then returned from the state of Qi to enter the state was merely him leveraging the power of a great state to contend for the throne; it was also not done with the intention of punishing the murderers. Therefore, the records state that he "entered" to highlight his guilt.

<margin>Lao Qiao of Nanfeng wrote a record.</margin>
His younger brother Yingchen and younger brother Xining inquired about the imperial examinations; he served as Assistant Prefect of Yongzhou.
Liu Yingchen removed the strange rocks in the pools and the water monsters of the Yuxi River, for which the people were very grateful.
Liu Xue, former Prefect of Luzhou, was promoted to Military Commissioner of Dongchuan for his merits in defending Chengdu. At that time, the Southern Nanzhao once again invaded Lizhou. They sent a letter to the Western Sichuan circuit requesting passage to see the Son of Heaven to plead their grievances.
Liu Xue urged the Military Commissioner, Niu Cong, to behead forty of their envoys.
He kept only two people, gave them a letter, branded them, and insulted them; the barbarians then retreated.

Liu Ping, courtesy name Ziyi, was a man of Wuling. During the Yuanyou era <note>1086–1094</note>, he served as Prefect of Jiangxi. At that time, in Jiangxi, only the Jun <note>a region</note> did not submit to litigation, so the prefect was known as the Governor of the Jiangxi Daoist Temple. When Ziyi arrived, the administration became even more clear and simple, gradually reaching a point of having no lawsuits. He built a new hall for leisure and planted *nanmu* <gloss>a type of fine cedar</gloss> trees.
He renovated the Jiangxi Daoist Temple to encourage its customs, and the common people were pleased.

Liu Yue, courtesy name Yuanli, was from Huating. He was by nature exceptionally filial and deeply learned in the Confucian Classics. During the Daguan era <note>1107–1110</note>, he became a scholar at the Imperial Academy and served as a professor in Bazhou. In the early Jingkang era <note>1126–1127</note>, he became a Palace Censor, arguing that the three surveillance commissioners should not be abandoned. Later, holding the title of Attendant at the Dragon Diagram Pavilion, he served as Prefect of Yanzhou and concurrent Military Commissioner for the Zhexi circuit. When the Jin people invaded, the various commanderies were shaken with fear, but Yue stood firm and defended his isolated territory.

The stele of Prefect Fan of Lujiang contains ten seal-script characters. Prefect Fan, whose name was Shi and style name was Juqing, appears in the "Biographies of Singular Conduct" in the *Book of the Later Han*. This stele was erected by the magistrate of the county, Mr. Xue, and the local townsman Zhai Xun, who built a shrine and set up the stone. The *Record of Metal and Stone* states that the *Essential Record of Calligraphy* attributes it to the hand of Cai Yong. However, examining the stele, it was erected in the third year of the Qinglong reign of the Wei dynasty <note>235 CE</note>, and is therefore not the writing of Cai. The *Explanation of Clerical Script* notes that although this stele does not reach the standard of the four inscriptions from the Yankang and Huangchu reigns, among other Wei-dynasty steles, it is still worth noting. Li Sizhen of the Tang dynasty, in his *Postscript on Calligraphy*, claimed that among all the styles by Master Cai, the Stele of Fan Juqing is the most elegant and refined, standing unrivaled throughout the ages. Huang Xiao
A man from Nancheng. He became a <term>jinshi</term> <gloss>a successful candidate in the imperial examinations</gloss> during the Dazhong reign period. He drifted through minor official appointments for twenty years. He once said that a great man should strive to distinguish himself, and how could one be content with a mediocre life serving under others. He served as a vice-magistrate in Luzhou. When the Transport Commissioner Chen Gao used his authority to intimidate the officials under his command, an official brought a lawsuit against Gao. The imperial court sent Xiao to guard the crisis. Although Xiao was a subordinate, the situation was extremely critical, yet Xiao handled it with reason and did not concern himself with the threats. Observers were filled with admiration.
He attained the position of Assistant Secretary in the Bureau of Operations.

Huang Zhen
Courtesy name Boqi. A man from Pucheng. He passed the imperial examinations and was promoted successively to the position of Erudite of the Imperial Library. He served as vice-magistrate of Chuan. When the troops plotted a mutiny, the others did not dare to intervene. Zhen spoke to the official in charge, saying, "Has the imperial court forgotten the Eastern Sichuan region? This is merely a matter of waiting for the official imperial decrees." He immediately opened the prefectural treasury and distributed funds just as they had done in Western Sichuan. The unrest was settled. The following day, the imperial decree arrived. Later, he was promoted from Assistant Secretary in the Ministry of Justice to Transport Commissioner of the Jianghuai region. Prior to this, Li Pu had risen from a minor clerk in the Three Offices to serve as Transport Commissioner for over ten years. His corruption and crimes were rampant. Ding Wei supported him, and no one dared to speak out. Before Zhen departed for his post, he submitted a memorial to the throne to explain his own position. His language was quite indignant. Emperor Zhenzong knew that he had no ulterior motives. Zhen discussed this with the Emperor, saying, "Your Majesty should maintain harmony with the officials." Zhen replied, "To uphold justice and serve as a loyal minister is the duty of a subject. If a person fails the responsibilities entrusted by Your Majesty, I dare not maintain harmony with them." Upon his arrival at the transport office, he investigated dozens of cases of corruption and graft. Those who were sentenced and dismissed were numerous.

This stele was erected by the County Magistrate, Lord Xue, and the local villagers, including Zhai Xun, to establish a shrine and monument. The *Explanation of Clerical Script* <note>original: "Lishi"</note> states that although this stele does not reach the level of the four inscriptions from the Yankang and Huangchu eras, it is the most commendable among other Wei dynasty steles. Li Sizhen of the Tang dynasty, in his *Sequel to the Evaluation of Calligraphy* <note>original: "Shuhou Pin"</note>, claimed that among all of Master Cai's works, the stele of Fan Juqing is the most elegant and brilliant, unsurpassed by any in ancient or modern times. Regarding the idea that "one can achieve merit through diligence," <note>referencing a passage from the Classic of History</note> Gao Yao said: "I have no knowledge; I only think to assist and provide guidance." The commentary states: "I have no personal knowledge, and I have not been able to think of ways to achieve virtue. I merely recount and present the events of antiquity, and because of this, Yu praised him and accepted his humble words." The sequence of sounds and meanings: "knowledge" <term>zhi</term> is read as written, with Xu’s pronunciation as <term>wei</term>; Ma’s pronunciation is <term>zhi</term>. "Think" <term>si</term> is read as written, with Xu’s pronunciation as <term>xi</term> and <term>li</term>, and the sound as <term>yang</term>. The sub-commentary states: "This refers to acceptance. Ma says it means to praise/follow."

Regarding the statement that "what one should strive for is to examine the words of others," when people speak of what is good, the will of Heaven returns rewards. Furthermore, the bright virtue of Heaven relies on the eyes and ears of the people. When the people speak of what is good, Heaven sees and hears; observe those who possess virtue and employ our people. Use this to revere the majesty of Heaven; use it among those in high and low positions, not avoiding the noble or the base. Therefore, one must be reverent. The ruler of the land holds the majesty of Heaven; regarding rewards and punishments, one must not deviate from the high and low, nor avoid the noble or the base. Therefore, one must be reverent. 

Gao Yao, having presented this admonition, wished for it to be implemented, and thus said: "My words here accord with the ancient path and can be put into practice; they cannot be neglected." Yu immediately accepted them, saying: "Yes, your words are practical and one can achieve merit through them. You have been able to think and reach the point of deep admonition." The Emperor and Gao Yao then accepted these with humility, saying: "I have no knowledge and have not been able to think of ways to achieve goodness. I have merely recounted and presented the events of antiquity, that is all."

<summary>This passage discusses the dialogue between the legendary figures Yu the Great and Gao Yao regarding the responsibilities of a ruler, emphasizing humility, the importance of listening to the people, and the practice of governing through ancient precedents.</summary>

To speak of realizing merit, Gao Yao said, "I have no knowledge, but I think, and I merely assist. Is it not so?" The commentary says: I do not yet possess knowledge, nor have I been able to think and bring things to goodness; I merely assist in reporting the affairs of the ancients and speak of them. Because Yu praised him, he followed with humble words to speak of it. Note on pronunciation and meaning: 
"Fear" <term>wei</term> <gloss>fear/awe</gloss> is read as written, Xu reads it as "majesty"; Ma uses "majesty". "Knowledge" <term>zhi</term> <gloss>know</gloss> is read as written, Xu reads it as "wisdom". "Think" <term>si</term> <gloss>think</gloss> is read as written, Xu reads it as "sih" (the reverse of "official"). "Assist" <term>xiang</term> <gloss>assist</gloss> is read as "sih-yang", meaning "to follow." Ma says it means "to rely on." The <term>Erya</term> <gloss>Dictionary of Progress</gloss> uses the character <term>rang</term>, meaning "to rely on," read as "yang."

Commentary:
The correct meaning is that this follows the previous phrase "Exert yourself!" It speaks of that which one should exert oneself in. Because Heaven's intelligence and brilliance observe through the senses of the people, if you use our people as your ears and eyes, and through this intelligence examine the virtuous words of the people, the will of Heaven will return rewards. Furthermore, Heaven's brilliant virtue is to be feared; those who act against the way of Heaven are observed through the reports of the people and are subsequently punished and attacked, thus fulfilling Heaven's brilliant majesty. That which Heaven rewards and punishes reaches both high and low, avoiding neither the noble nor the base, so one must be reverent. As a ruler with territory, Gao Yao has already presented this admonition, wishing for his words to be taken to heart, thus he says, "These words of mine conform to the ancient Way and can be realized in practice; they must not be neglected." Yu immediately accepted this and said, "Yes, your words are useful and can be realized to establish merit." He emphasized his words to provide a deep warning. Gao Yao then responded with humility, saying, "I do not yet possess knowledge, nor have I been able to think and bring things to goodness. What I have said is merely to assist in reporting what was done in ancient times; it is not..."

Words on how one may establish merit. Gao Yao said, "I have no wisdom. I only think to aid and support." The commentary says, "I have not yet attained knowledge, nor have I been able to think and extend myself toward what is good. I merely support and present the practices of the ancients and speak of them. Because of Yu's praise, I respond with humble words."

The preface regarding sound and meaning:
"Fear" <note>original: 畏</note> is read as written, Xu reads it as "awe." Ma reads it as "awe." "Knowledge" <note>original: 知</note> is read as written, Xu reads it as "wisdom." "Think" <note>original: 思</note> is read as written, Xu reads it with the phonetic <term>xi-li</term> <gloss>a modern spelling guide for pronunciation</gloss>. "Support" <note>original: 襄</note> is read with the phonetic <term>xi-yang</term> <gloss>meaning 'to rise' or 'to assist'</gloss>. Ma says it means "to rely upon." According to the <term>Erya</term> <gloss>a dictionary of archaic terms</gloss>, it is written as <term>rang</term> <gloss>a variant character for 'to assist'</gloss>, meaning "to rely upon."

Sub-commentary:
The correct interpretation is that this follows the preceding section on "diligently laboring." The substance of this exhortation is that Heaven’s intelligence, in observing the people, sees those who possess virtue and utilizes the intelligence of our people as its ears and eyes. When it observes those who speak good words, the will of Heaven grants them rewards. Furthermore, Heaven’s bright virtue is something to be feared. As for Heaven’s awe, it utilizes the words of our people to identify those who are evil and rebellious, and thereupon punishes and strikes them, thereby fulfilling its brilliant awe. The rewards and punishments of Heaven reach both high and low without avoiding the noble or the base. Therefore, one must be respectful. As for the ruler of the land, once Gao Yao had presented these warnings, he desired that his words be taken to heart; thus, he said, "These words of mine are in accord with the ancient path; they can be put into practice and must not be neglected." Yu then accepted them, saying, "Indeed, your words are practical and can lead to the establishment of merit." He weighed these words heavily as a profound warning. Gao Yao then responded with humility, saying, "I have no knowledge, and I have not been able to think and bring myself to what is good. What I have said is merely to support and present the practices of the ancients and speak of them; it is not..."

Regarding what can be realized to establish merit, Gao Yao said: I have no knowledge; I only think to aid and support. The commentary says: I have not yet attained knowledge, nor have I been able to think of ways to reach what is good. I merely support and present the practices of the ancient sages to speak of them. Because Yu praised this, he followed up with these humble words. The preface to the pronunciation and meaning says: 
"Fear" <term>wei</term> <gloss>fear/awe</gloss>: read as the character, Xu reads it as <term>wei</term> <gloss>awe</gloss>; Ma's version uses <term>wei</term> <gloss>awe</gloss>. "Know" <term>zhi</term> <gloss>knowledge</gloss>: read as the character, Xu reads it as <term>zhi</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss>. "Think" <term>si</term> <gloss>to think</gloss>: read as the character, Xu reads it as <term>xi-li</term> <gloss>a phonetic reading</gloss>. "Aid" <term>xiang</term> <gloss>to assist/help</gloss>: read as <term>xi-yang</term> <gloss>a phonetic reading</gloss>, meaning to help; Ma says it means to follow. Note: In the <term>Erya</term> <gloss>a dictionary of synonyms</gloss> it is written as <term>rang</term> <gloss>to follow/rely on</gloss>, meaning to follow, read as <term>ru-yang</term> <gloss>a phonetic reading</gloss>.

Sub-commentary:
The orthodox meaning states: This follows the "exert yourself" from above, discussing what one should exert oneself in. With Heaven's brilliance, it observes people's virtue through its own vision; it uses the intelligence of our people as its ears and eyes to discern those who speak of goodness, and Heaven's will is to reward them. Moreover, Heaven's brilliant virtue is to be feared. Heaven's majesty lies in using the words of our people to discern evil and those who rebel, then punishing and attacking them to fulfill its brilliant awe. The rewards and punishments of Heaven reach both high and low, not avoiding the noble or the base; thus, one must be reverent. For a ruler possessing territory, Gao Yao, having laid out this warning, wished for the ruler to take these words to heart, and so he said: These words of mine conform to the ancient path, and can be realized in practice; they must not be neglected. Yu then accepted this, saying: Indeed, your words can be used to establish merit. By emphasizing his words, he provided a profound warning to the Emperor. Gao Yao then followed this with humility, saying: I have no knowledge, and have not been able to think of how to reach what is good. What I have said is merely a support and presentation of what was practiced in high antiquity; nothing more.

<summary>This text contains a sub-commentary on the Classic of History, specifically Gao Yao's humble advice to Emperor Yu regarding the importance of understanding Heaven's moral governance and the necessity of personal humility in leadership.</summary>

Listen carefully, listen carefully. The crowd all dispersed. One day, a Brahmin monk suddenly arrived from the sky. The Master asked, "Where did you just come from?" The monk replied, "From the Western Heavens." The Master asked, "When did you leave there?" The Brahmin replied, "This morning." The Master said, "You are very late." The Brahmin replied, "I was enjoying the mountains and water." The Master said, "Supernatural powers and play are certainly present, but you are not clear." The Brahmin said, "I came specifically to the Eastern lands to pay respects to Manjushri, and instead I have met a little Shakyamuni." He then produced several dozen palm leaves <note>referring to *pattra* or palm-leaf manuscripts</note> with Sanskrit script, offered them to the Master, paid his respects, and rode the sky away. From then on, the Master was called the "Little Shakyamuni."

In the second year of the Zhenming era of the Ma Liang <note>referring to the Later Liang dynasty</note>, the year Bingzi, the Master moved to Dongping and spoke a verse: "Seventy-seven years have passed, impermanence is today. The sun is at its zenith, my hands embrace my knees." Having spoken, he held his knees and passed away. The following year, his Dharma-heir, Chan Master Nanta Guangyong, moved the remains back to Yangshan and built a pagoda beneath Jiyun Peak, bestowing the posthumous title "Chan Master Zhitong, Pagoda of Miraculous Light." The Master was a successor to Chan Master Weishan You; his teaching flourished, and everyone honored him as the "Great Yangshan School."

Ji Chu first resided at Wangmang Mountain. In the sixth year of the Xiantong era of the Xizong Emperor, the mountain spirit said, "In the southeast, there is a blessed land called Great Yangshan." The Master then moved there.

In the year Jiaxu, the eighth year of the Dazhong era, there was a monk on Zhongnan Mountain who built a hut to practice meditation. One day, a monkey stole his *kasaya* <note>monastic robe</note>, put it on, and sat in meditation. Subsequently, a group of monkeys all practiced sitting in meditation, and some even passed away while doing so. To this day, there are five monkey pagodas. Upon hearing this, the Xuanzong Emperor composed a eulogy: "Alas, you monkeys, able to enter meditation. The heart-ape has been unmoved for thousands of springs. You stopped climbing the red trees in the winter of the third year."

<note>Imperial Collection of the Four Treasuries</note>
<note>Shi Shi Ji Gu Lue, Volume Three</note>

People then harbor their populations, drive off their livestock, cut down their trees, and destroy their palaces. Can the *Spring and Autumn Annals* <note>the classic Confucian chronicle of the state of Lu</note> consistently record these as invasions?

In the sixth year, the people of Zheng came to report the termination of peace. The <term>Guliang Zhuan</term> <gloss>Guliang Commentary</gloss> states that reporting the termination of peace means it did not come to a successful conclusion. Its intention is to suggest that previously, Lu and Zheng were at peace; however, in the fourth year, the state of Lu led a host to attack Zheng, so the people of Zheng came to request the end of the former peace. This is incorrect. Whenever "peace" is mentioned, it generally refers to an agreement between two states not to turn against one another. Now, since Lu attacked Zheng, the end of the peace is obvious. If the people of Zheng had not come to report the termination of peace, could we have claimed the old peace was still intact? Can a state attack another and still claim there is peace? Thus, it is clear that the peace between Lu and Zheng was broken without waiting for a formal notification, and there is no question of a failed attempt to conclude the matter.

<summary>Liu Chang analyzes the diplomatic implications of reporting the termination of peace in the Spring and Autumn Annals, arguing that acts of war automatically invalidate previous peace agreements.</summary>

Those that are partial and obstructed become objects, which is why some are noble and others are base, and they cannot be made uniform. When those base things become objects, they are already fettered by the partiality and obstruction of their physical form and vitality, and they lack the means to fulfill the completeness of their original substance. Only the birth of a human being attains the correctness and fluidity of this vitality; thus, their nature is the most noble. Consequently, within their hearts, they are empty, spiritual, and penetrating, and all principles are fully prepared. This is precisely how they differ from birds and beasts; it is also the source of their ability to become like Yao or Shun <note>Legendary sage-kings of ancient China</note> and to participate with Heaven and Earth in supporting the work of transformation and nurture. This is what is meant by the "Luminous Virtue" <note>A reference to the Great Learning, referring to the inherent clarity of the human mind.</note>. <note>Phonetic and Semantic Notes:
The "xing" in Xu Xing is pronounced like "heng." The "meng" below is pronounced like "geng," and refers to the common people. "He" (coarse clothing) is pronounced like "ji." "Kun" is pronounced like "kun." An commentary by Xu Shuzhong says: "kun" means to weave; the *Pi Cang* dictionary says "kun" means to imitate. The character written with the "wood" radical is an error. "Xia" is pronounced like "zhuo," meaning to strike. "Chen Xiang" is a name; "Ding" says the level and departing tones are both acceptable. "Yong" and "sun" (referring to cooked meals) are used together. "Shen" is in the departing tone. "Cu" (coarse) is pronounced like the character "cu," and the note later is the same. "Yu" is pronounced like "yu," and the following "yu" is the same. "She" is pronounced like "she," meaning to stop. "Lu" (road) is read as "lu" (dew). "Lei" is pronounced like "lei"; the character is also written as "lei." "Shi" (to eat) is read as "si." "Shi yu ren" (to eat the food of others) is read as written. "Si" is pronounced like "fan." "Bi" is pronounced like "bi." "Yue" (the river name) is read as "yao." "Zhong" is pronounced like "li." "Xia" is read as "he." Writing it as "shi" (wet) is an error. "Gu" is pronounced like "gu." "Qi" is pronounced like "xue." "Fang" is pronounced like "wang." "Yue" (said) is pronounced like "si"; some versions use "ri" (day), which is an error. "Lao" and "lai" (to toil/to encourage) are both in the departing tone. "Bu yu yan" (not involved in it) is pronounced like "yu," and is also read as written. "Bei" (to double) is explained by Ding as meaning "xie" (together), a case of an ancient character being borrowed. "Zhi" and "ren" (office/responsibility) are pronounced like "zhen."</note>

If prices are made the same, it will lead to a path of contention and disorder in the world. "Ju" <note>large</note> refers to coarse sandals, "xiao" <note>small</note> refers to fine sandals. If they are sold for the same price, who would be willing to make the fine ones? In that case, Master Xu is merely teaching people to be deceitful. How could he possibly govern a state?

<note>Pronunciation and Meaning</note>
"Hang" in Xu Hang is pronounced like the character "heng" <note>constant/horizontal</note>. "Xia" <note>below</note> in Mengxia is pronounced with the "meng" initial and "xia" final, same for the following. "Zhong" <note>heel</note> is pronounced like "long". "Meng" <note>common people</note> is pronounced like "geng". "Yi" <note>clothing</note> is pronounced like "he". "Kun" <note>weaving/thatching</note> is pronounced like "kun". Xu Shuzhong says: "Kun" means to weave. The *Pi Cang* dictionary says: "Kun" means to imitate. The version written with the character "cai" <note>talent</note> and "mu" <note>wood</note> is incorrect. Zhang writes it as "yin", same pronunciation. "Xia" is pronounced like "zhuo" <note>to strike</note>. "Chen Xiang" is pronounced with the "ding" initial; "qu" and "ping" are both acceptable. "Yong" <note>cooked meal</note> and "sun" <note>cooked millet</note>. "Dang shen" is pronounced with the "ding" initial in the departing tone. "Cu" <note>coarse</note> is pronounced like "cu"; the subsequent notes are the same. "Yu" <note>together with</note> is pronounced like "yu"; the following "yu" is the same. "She" <note>to reside/stop</note> is pronounced like "she" <note>to forgive</note>. "Lu" <note>road</note>: Zhang says "lu" is the same as "lu" <note>dew</note>. "Lei" is pronounced like "wei"; the character is also written as "lei", pronounced like "lang guo". "Shi ren zhi shi" <note>eating the food of others</note>, "shi" is pronounced like "si". "Shi yu ren" <note>eating at the place of others</note> is read as written. "Fan" <note>overflowing</note> is pronounced like "fan". "Bi" <note>press/oppress</note> is pronounced like "bi". "Yue ji luo" <note>to boil/soak/river name</note>: Ding says the first is pronounced like "yao", the middle is pronounced like "zi li", the last is pronounced like "ta he"; writing it as "shi" <note>damp</note> is incorrect. "Gu" <note>wailing</note> is pronounced like "gu". "Qi" is pronounced like "xue". "Fang" <note>to release</note> is pronounced like "fang wang". "Yue" is pronounced like "si"; some write it as "ri" <note>sun</note>, which is incorrect. "Lao zhi lai zhi" <note>to encourage and invite them</note>: Ding says both are in the departing tone. "Bu yu yan" <note>not participating in it</note>, the "yu" is pronounced like "yu" <note>leisure/participate</note>, read as written. "Bei zhi" <note>to double it</note>: Ding says the meaning should be "xie" <note>together</note>; it is an ancient character used as a loan word. "Bei" <note>to double</note> is the same as "zi bei". "Zhi ren" <note>to govern/appoint</note> is pronounced like "ren".

"Yong" <note>cooked meal</note> is pronounced "yong"; "sun" <note>evening meal</note> is pronounced "sun". "Bi" <note>to press/compel</note> is pronounced "bi" <note>as in *bī*</note>. "Yue" <note>to boil/soak</note> in "Ji" and "Luo" is pronounced "yao" <note>as in *yuè/yào*</note>. The middle character is pronounced "li" <note>as in *lǐ*</note>. The final character is pronounced "he" <note>as in *hé*</note>; writing it as "shi" <note>damp</note> is incorrect. <unclear>&KR0561;</unclear> is pronounced "gu". "Lao" <note>to labor/comfort</note> in "lao zhi lai zhi" <note>to comfort them, to encourage them</note> is pronounced in the departing tone <note>fourth tone</note>. His wife brought three daughters, all of whom were already grown. Zhou treated them as his own children. Later, the wife was cruel and jealous. Zhou had long kept several maidservants, two of whom became pregnant. The wife, for other reasons, whipped and beat them without a single day of respite. The two maids, both pregnant, often used their backs, arms, or legs to take the lashes, while the wife frequently used a staff to strike their abdomens, wishing them to be incomplete <note>meaning to cause a miscarriage or fetal injury</note>. The two maids eventually suffered miscarriages and died from the whippings and beatings.

After killing the two maids, the three daughters were married off one after another. Because of official duties, the family temporarily resided in Hengyang and did not return for five years. All three of his daughters died during childbirth. Each time a daughter died, the wife would offer meals to monks to repent for her previous actions of whipping the pregnant maids, and she would read scriptures and perform the rituals of the <term>Liang Wudi Chan</term> <gloss>The Repentance Ritual of Emperor Wu of Liang</gloss>. All three daughters died in childbirth; before they died, they all spent ten days crying out in agony, twisting and turning before finally expiring. The wife wept, worried, and fell ill. A year or so after her daughters passed away, she also died. Alas.

<summary>This passage recounts the moral retribution experienced by a woman who cruelly abused her pregnant maidservants, subsequently suffering the loss of her three daughters in childbirth and her own eventual death.</summary>

Yet, all three daughters died in childbirth; before they died, they all spent ten days crying out in agony, writhing in pain before they eventually passed away. If prices are made uniform, it will create a path of contention and disorder in the world. *Ju* <note>a large type of sandal</note> refers to coarse sandals, while *xiao* refers to fine sandals.

If people were forced to sell them at the same price, who would be willing to craft the fine ones? At the time, Master Xu was merely teaching people to be deceitful. How could such a person govern a state?

**Phonetic and Semantic Annotations**

Regarding the conduct of Xu Xing: *Ding* reads it as *heng* (to move/flow), also read as *xia meng qie* (to meet), same below. *Zhong* (to follow on the heels of) is read as *long qie*. *Meng* (people/populace) is read as *wang geng qie*, same as *mang*. *Yi* (clothing made of coarse hemp) is read as *he yu ji qie*, same below. *Kun* (to weave) is read as *ding yin kun*. Note: Xu Shuzhong says *kun* means to weave. The *Picang* dictionary says *kun* means to imitate. The version written with the radical for 'material' (才) and 'wood' (木) is an error. Zhang writes it as *yin* (cushion), the pronunciation is the same. *Xie* (to strike) is read as *ding yin zhuo*, meaning to strike. It uses the radical for 'material' (才) beside the character for 'pig' (豕). Regarding Chen Xiang, *Ding* says the flat and falling tones are both acceptable. *Yong* (to cook) is read as *yong*. *Sun* (the evening meal) is read as *sun*. *Dang shen* (to handle by oneself) is read by *Ding* in the falling tone. *Cu* (coarse) is read as *cu*; subsequent notes use the same. *Zhi yu* (the final particle 'yu') is read as *yu*; the same applies to 'yu' (与) below. *She* (to stop/rest) in all instances is read as *ding yin she*, meaning to stop. *Lu* (road/dew): *Ding* and Zhang both say *lu* is the same as *lu* (dew). *Lei* (thin/emaciated) is read as *li wei qie*; the character is also written as *lei*, read as *lang guo qie*. *Shi* in "eating the food of others" is read as *si*. In "eating at the table of others," it is read according to the character. *Si* is read as *fan*. *Bi* is read as *bi*. *Yue* (to boil) in "Ji-Luo" <note>names of rivers</note>: *Ding* says the first character is read as *yao*, the second as *zi li qie*, and the third as *ta he qie*; the version written as *shi* (wet) is an error. *Gu* (wailing sound) is read as *gu*. *Xie* (carving/contract) is read as *xue*. *Fang* (to release/exile) is read as *fang wang qie*. *Yue* (to say) is read by *Ding* as *si*; some write it as *ri*, which is an error. *Lao zhi lai zhi* (to toil for them and encourage them): *Ding* says both are read in the falling tone. *Bu yu yan* (not participating in it): the latter character is read as *yu*, or according to the character. *Bei zhi* (to double it): *Ding* says the intended meaning should be *xie* (together/uniform), and the ancient character was borrowed for this usage; the same applies to the *bei* in the subsequent *zi bei*. *Zhi ren* (to govern one’s responsibilities/duties) is read by *Ding* as *er zhen qie*.

Weiyang was established as Meng Prefecture during the Western Wei dynasty. During the Renshou reign of the Sui dynasty, it was renamed Wei Prefecture and also served as the seat of Weiyang Commandery. In the Tang dynasty, it became a county under the jurisdiction of Jin Prefecture. The stele, erected in the first year of the Renshou reign, still bears the name Meng Prefecture, but it was soon changed to Wei Prefecture. The stele does not record the name of the author or the calligrapher, yet the brushwork is vigorous and elegant, causing one to lose track of time while admiring it. Since the Kaihuang and Renshou eras, many steles and inscriptions feature excellent calligraphy, though the names of the creators are often omitted. Only Ding Daohu frequently signed his own work, yet very few of his stele stones remain. I have often lamented this with Cai Junmo. After the Daye era, the calligraphy of the Sui official <term>Shuai Geng</term> <gloss>a title referring to Ouyang Xun</gloss> and Yu Shinan began to flourish, and upon entering the Tang dynasty, it achieved great prominence.

It was Yuyang, where the Western Wei established Meng Prefecture. During the Ren-shou era of the Sui dynasty, it was changed to Yu Prefecture, and it also served as the seat of Yuyang Commandery. From the Da-ye era <note>605–618 CE</note> onward, the calligraphy of Shuai-geng <note>Ouyang Xun, known by his title Shuai-geng</note> and Yu Shinan began to flourish, and once they connected with the Tang dynasty, their styles became widely celebrated. If one is outside the palace, then there is no taboo; therefore, when a subject is in the presence of the ruler, there is no taboo. Lu Dalin stated: Those who are of great mourning or small mourning are not tabooed because the obligation of grace is light. Chen Hao stated: The taboo of a wife and the taboo of a woman both refer to the ancestors of their respective families.

General Discussion: Tian Qiong stated: In the *Zaji* <note>Record of Miscellaneous Customs</note>, it is said that a mother’s taboo is kept within the palace, and a wife’s taboo is not mentioned in her presence. That this woman’s taboo is the same as the mother’s taboo is because the *Zaji* distinguishes between the honorable and the humble; this text speaks of it in general terms regarding when one does not go outside the gate.

If an older brother is obedient, after he is capped, his mother and brothers bow to him, holding him accountable for the conduct of filial piety and brotherly respect. When a lord or a village official or an esteemed village elder presents him as an adult, they hold him accountable for the conduct of loyalty and obedience. Once the conduct of loyalty and obedience is established, the person’s character is cultivated and the way of humanity is complete; thus, he is fit to be a person. When the way of humanity is complete within oneself, one extends this to govern the state; thus, one is fit to govern others. The sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity wished to hold people accountable in this manner, and therefore the divination said: "Divining for a guest is to show respect for him," which is the very means of placing a heavy responsibility upon him. Among the five rites, the joyful rites occupy the end, and among the joyful rites, the capping ceremony is placed first. To speak of the capping ceremony as the beginning of the rites is to understand the importance of this joyful occasion. Indeed, when applied to the capping, it is called a rite; when applied to the rites, it is called a task. Because they placed importance on this task, they performed it in the ancestral temple.

It was asked: The eye is the physical substance, and the light of the eye is the <term>po</term>. The ear is the physical substance; how can one identify the <term>po</term> of the ear? However, one should not define the <term>po</term> by the word "knowing." "Knowing" is something that resides in the mind. The mind can know, but whether something is sweet, bitter, salty, or bland must be experienced through the tongue. 　Someone asked how this is so. I replied: The physical spirit is the spirit of form; the soul is the spirit of qi <note>gloss: vital energy</note>. The soul and the physical spirit are the essences of form and energy. This is what is meant by numinosity. Therefore, Master Zhang <note>note: Zhang Zai, a prominent Neo-Confucian philosopher</note> said: "The innate capacity <note>original: "liangneng"</note> of the two energies." For instance, the experience of sweet, bitter, salty, or bland must pass through the tongue. When an elderly person becomes hard of hearing or their vision grows dim, it is because their physical spirit is gradually dissipating.

Li Qi, in his poem *Excursion by Boat on the Ji River with Various Gentlemen*, writes: "The shallow and the deep reveal the duckweed and the algae growing."

Guanxiu

In his *Poem on Suffering Heat*, he writes: "Desiring to create smoke."

Gravel

In the *Book of Han*, biography of Huo Qubing: Zhao Xin advised the Chanyu, saying, "If the Han army crosses the desert, their men and horses will be exhausted. The Xiongnu can capture them with ease." He ordered the baggage train to retreat far to the north, while keeping elite troops in wait north of the desert. When [Wei] Qing's army went beyond the frontier for over a thousand *li*, they saw the Chanyu’s troops arrayed and waiting. Wei Qing then ordered the armies of Wu and Liu to form circular camps and released five thousand cavalry to engage the Xiongnu. The Xiongnu sent ten thousand cavalry to meet them. As the sun was setting, a great wind arose, blowing directly into their faces, so that the two armies could not see each other. The Han further released their left and right wings to surround the Chanyu. The Chanyu saw that the Han army was numerous and their men and horses were still strong; the fighting was disadvantageous to the Xiongnu. At dusk, the Chanyu rode one of his six strong horses, accompanied by several hundred cavalry, and charged out to the northwest, escaping through the Han encirclement.

In the *Book of Jin*, biography of Ge Hong: "Pushed him away as being of humble status, yet sought a thousand pieces of gold."

In the *Book of Qi*, Record of the Henan Xiongnu: "The land is always windy and cold; when people walk on the level sand, the wind rises and obliterates their tracks." See also the record on windy and cold conditions under the record of the Di and Qiang in Henan.

In the *Song History*, Treatise on Food and Money: In the fourth year of the Qingyuan reign, an imperial decree was issued: "In all circuits, if there are uncultivated lands that have been reclaimed, if they cannot be farmed, the tax should be reduced or eliminated."

Li Qi's poem, "Traveling by Boat on the Ji River with Gentlemen": The shallow and deep are covered with dew, and duckweed and algae grow.

Void.

Li Yi's "Song of Watering Horses": I ask the old man by the spring, when shall we see each other?

Guanxiu, "Poem on Bitter Heat": The rice and hemp must bear fruit; one wishes to sprout smoke and gravel.

*History of the Han*, Biography of Huo Qubing: Zhao Xin advised the Chanyu <note>the ruler of the Xiongnu</note>, saying: "If the Han troops cross the desert, their men and horses will be exhausted, and the Xiongnu can capture them with ease." He then moved everything far to the north, keeping the supply wagons and elite troops waiting north of the desert. They happened to meet Qing's army. Having gone a thousand li beyond the border, they saw the Chanyu's troops arranged in battle formation. Thereupon, Qing ordered the army of Wu Liu to form a defensive circle, and sent five thousand cavalry to engage the Xiongnu. The Xiongnu sent ten thousand cavalry to meet them. As the sun was setting, a great wind arose, blowing into their faces so that the two armies could not see one another. The Han sent more troops to flank the left and right, encircling the Chanyu. The Chanyu saw that the Han army was numerous and that their men and horses were still strong; the battle was disadvantageous to the Xiongnu. At dusk, the Chanyu mounted six lean but strong horses, followed by about a hundred men, and charged directly to the northwest, breaking through the Han encirclement and galloping away.

*History of the Jin*, Biography of Ge Hong: Pushing aside his lowly status, he sought a thousand pieces of gold in the marketplace.

*History of the Qi*, Biography of the Henan Xiongnu: The land is constantly windy and cold. When people walk in the level sands, their footprints are obliterated as they are blown away. See also: "Biography of the Henan Di and Qiang," under "Wind and Cold."

*History of the Song*, Treatise on Food and Money: In the fourth year of the Qingyuan reign, an edict was issued to all circuits to stop the forced sale of fields, to restore and reduce the tax price, and to remove those lands that could not be cultivated.

*Dharma Collection Sutra*: Good son, if there are beings who should be conquered with superiority.

(Harmonious void, Li Qi’s poem on traveling to the Ji River and boating: “The shallow and the deep reveal the <term>hollow void</term> <gloss>empty space/emptiness</gloss>, where water weeds grow.” Li Yi’s poem “Drinking Horses at the Spring”: “I ask the old man at the spring, when will I see the <term>hollow void</term> <gloss>emptiness</gloss> again?” Guan Xiu)
(Poem on Bitter Heat: “Rice and hemp must bear fruit; the <term>hollow void</term> <gloss>emptiness/haze</gloss> begins to produce smoke.”)
Gravel (Book of Han, Biography of Huo Qubing: Zhao Xin advised the Shanyu <note>leader of the Xiongnu</note>, saying that if the Han army crossed the desert, their men and horses would be exhausted, and the Xiongnu could capture them easily. He then moved their heavy baggage far to the north and waited with elite troops north of the desert. Coincidentally, they met Wei Qing’s army, which had traveled over a thousand miles beyond the frontier. They saw the Shanyu’s army lined up and waiting. Wei Qing ordered the Wu Gang military chariots to form a ring as a camp and released five thousand cavalrymen to engage the Xiongnu. The Xiongnu also sent ten thousand cavalry to meet them. When the sun was about to set, a great wind rose, and <term>sand and gravel</term> <gloss>blinding dust/grit</gloss> struck their faces. The two armies could not see each other. The Han army further sent out their left and right wings to encircle the Shanyu. The Shanyu saw the Han army was numerous and their men and horses were still strong; the battle was unfavorable for the Xiongnu. At dusk, the Shanyu boarded a carriage drawn by six strong mules, accompanied by several hundred cavalry, and broke through the northwest of the Han encirclement, galloping away. Book of Jin, Biography of Ge Hong: “Pushing aside a humble background of <term>sand and gravel</term> <gloss>common/lowly material</gloss>, seeking a thousand pieces of gold.” Book of Qi, Biography of the Henan Xiongnu: “The land is constantly windy and cold; when people walk in the level sand, <term>sand and gravel</term> <gloss>grit/dust</gloss> fly up and the tracks are all erased.” Also see under “Wind and Cold” in the Biography of the Henan Di and Qiang tribes. Song History, Treatise on Food and Money: “In the fourth year of Qingyuan, an edict was issued to all circuits: if land offered for sale cannot be sold, or if land is reclaimed and the price is reduced, those areas of <term>sand and gravel</term> <gloss>barren land</gloss> that cannot be farmed shall be exempted.” Dharma Collection Sutra: “Good men, if all living beings should be superior...”
